answer: To block your IP addresses and exclude your own visits from your stats, go into the site settings of the website you'd like to block your activity from [1]. Choose IP Addresses in the Shields entry in the left-hand menu [1]. Click on the Add IP Address button to add a new address to the block list [1].

evidence.title: Exclude internal traffic from your analytics
evidence.text:
* Go into the site settings of the website you'd like to block your activity from

* Choose **IP Addresses** in the **Shields** entry in the left-hand menu

* Click on the **Add IP Address** button to add a new address to the block list

* You can manually insert an IP address (both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are acceptable) or you can click to block your current public IP address which our system will find and display for you

Plausible Shields modal to add an IP address to the block list with a description

* You can also add a description to help you identify which device or location you have blocked

* You need to add one IP address at a time and it has to be the full IP address as IP ranges are not supported. You can block up to 30 different IP addresses per website

Note: Block both IPv4 and IPv6 if your device uses both
Most modern devices and networks have both an IPv4 address (e.g. `203.0.113.5`) and an IPv6 address (e.g. `2001:db8::1`). Your browser or network proxy may send visits using either one depending on the connection.

If you block only your IPv4 address but your browser sends a request over IPv6, that visit will still be recorded. To reliably exclude your traffic, check whether your device has both address types and add each one separately.

The **block your current IP** button captures whichever address your browser is currently using. Click it, then visit a site like whatismyipaddress.com to check whether you also have a second address type, and add that manually if so.

* Once added to the block list, we will start blocking traffic from that specific IP address within a few minutes

* You can see the list of all the IP addresses that you're blocking at the moment. The entry in the list which has the **YOU** tag is your current IP address

* You can click the trash icon next to that IP address to remove it from the blocklist

* You can click the trash icon next to that IP address to remove it from the blocklist

question: I want to give a client a link that only shows traffic from one campaign and that they can't remove the filter from. Is that possible?
reference_answer: Yes. Create a shared link with the Limit to segment option, choosing a site segment. Viewers will always see data filtered by that segment and can't remove it, though they can add more filters on top of it. Only site segments, those anyone on your team can use, can be used.
key_facts: Shared links have a Limit to segment option
Viewers can't remove the segment but can add filters on top
Only site segments can be used
answer: If you enable this option, anyone who opens the dashboard using the shared link will always see data filtered by the selected segment only [1]. Viewers won't be able to remove that segment from the dashboard [1].

citations.quote: If you enable this option, anyone who opens the dashboard using the shared link will always see data filtered by the selected segment only.
Viewers won't be able to remove that segment from the dashboard.

evidence.title: Share your stats with a private and secure link
evidence.text:
If you enable this option, anyone who opens the dashboard using the shared link will always see data filtered by the selected segment only. Only site segments (i.e. segments that anyone on your team can use) can be used.

Viewers won't be able to remove that segment from the dashboard. They can see which filters are included in it and they can add more filters on top of it.

This makes it possible to share only the part of your analytics that matters to a specific audience. For example, you might want to share data only for visitors from a certain country or only for traffic related to a campaign. It prevents viewers from changing the base filters and seeing data you did not intend to share.

Info:
As an example, if the selected segment contains the filters "Country is Estonia or Poland" and "Page is not /private", visitors will be able to drill down further by adding "Country is Estonia" filter. If they try to go outside of the segment, by adding the filter "Country is Italy" as an example, they will see no data.

evidence.title: Dashboard FAQ
evidence.text:
If you've just installed Plausible and aren't seeing your own visits, there are a few common reasons:

- **WordPress plugin**: Our official WordPress plugin excludes logged-in admin visits by default. If the verification tool confirms the tracking is working, you have nothing to worry about.
- **Shields**: The Shields feature lets you block visits based on IP addresses, hostnames, countries or specific pages. Check whether you have any rules that might be excluding your own visits.
- **Adblockers**: If you're using a browser extension or network-level adblocker, it may be blocking the Plausible script. Consider setting up a proxy to serve the script as a first-party connection.

For more details, see our full troubleshooting guide.

evidence.title: Adding Plausible to WordPress
evidence.text: Our WordPress plugin excludes logged-in administrator visits by default. This is intentional. If you want to track your own visits, go to the "Track analytics for user roles" section in the plugin settings and enable the Administrator role.

question: Can I get bounce rate for each goal in a single API query?
reference_answer: No. Mixing the session metrics bounce_rate, views_per_visit and visit_duration with event dimensions such as event:goal isn't allowed. The only exceptions are event:page, and event:hostname when it is used together with event:page.
key_facts: Session metrics can't be mixed with event dimensions
bounce_rate, views_per_visit and visit_duration are session metrics
Exceptions are event:page and event:hostname with event:page
answer: Currently, it is only possible to break down on one property at a time [1]. Using a list of properties with one query is not supported [1].

citations.quote: Currently, it is only possible to break down on one property at a time.
Using a list of properties with one query is not supported.

evidence.title: Stats API v1 reference (legacy)
evidence.text: Currently, it is only possible to break down on one property at a time. Using a list of properties with one query is not supported. So if you want a breakdown by both `event:page` and `visit:source` for example, you would have to make multiple queries (break down on one property and filter on another) and then manually/programmatically group the results together in one report. This also applies for breaking down by time periods. To get a daily breakdown for every page, you would have to break down on `event:page` and make multiple queries for each date. For a simple time period breakdown, have a look at the Timeseries endpoint.

question: My Top Pages list shows /pricing and /pricing/ as two separate rows. How do I merge them?
reference_answer: The best fix is a 301 redirect so each page has a single address. If you can't change how your site handles URLs, you can merge them in your snippet with a `transformRequest` function that removes the trailing slash. It only affects pageviews sent after you add it, and you should update any pageview goal that ends with a slash.

question: My thank-you page keeps recording extra purchases when customers reload it. How do I stop the revenue being counted twice?
reference_answer: Reloaded thank-you pages fire the purchase event again and add more conversions and revenue. You can remove the trigger from the URL after sending using `history.replaceState`, send from a checkout callback instead of a page, ignore old checkouts on your server, or mark the order as tracked in your own store.
key_facts: Reloading a thank-you page can fire the purchase event again
Remove the trigger from the URL with history.replaceState after sending
Alternatively send from a callback, ignore old checkouts on the server or mark orders as tracked
answer:
To stop purchases from being counted twice when thank-you pages are reloaded, bookmarked, or reopened, you can use one of these approaches:
- If your page sends the event only when the URL carries a checkout ID or amount, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` right after `plausible(...)` [1]. A reload then has nothing to send [1]. No storage needed [1].
- Send from a callback, not a page [1]. Overlay checkouts (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) fire their success callback once per payment [1].
- Ignore old checkouts on the server [1]. When you look up the payment on your server, skip the event if the payment was created long ago (for example, Stripe's Checkout Session `created` timestamp is more than an hour old) [1].
- Mark the order in your own store [1]. If you already keep orders in a database, you can mark an order as tracked the first time the thank-you page renders, like our WordPress plugin does for WooCommerce orders [1]. Nothing extra is sent to Plausible [1].

citations.quote: - **Remove the trigger from the URL after sending.** If your page sends the event only when the URL carries a checkout ID or amount, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` right after `plausible(...)`. A reload then has nothing to send. No storage needed.
- **Send from a callback, not a page.** Overlay checkouts (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) fire their success callback once per payment.

- **Ignore old checkouts on the server.** When you look up the payment on your server, skip the event if the payment was created long ago (for example, Stripe's Checkout Session `created` timestamp is more than an hour old).

- **Mark the order in your own store.** If you already keep orders in a database, you can mark an order as tracked the first time the thank-you page renders, like our WordPress plugin does for WooCommerce orders. Nothing extra is sent to Plausible.

evidence.title: Ecommerce revenue and attribution tracking
evidence.text:
**One purchase event vs. per-product events**

The simplest approach is a single `Purchase` event with the total order value. This gives you clean revenue totals, referral attribution and conversion rates without complex setup.

If you need to break down revenue by product type, category or subscription tier, use custom properties alongside the revenue event. For example:

```js
plausible('Purchase', {revenue: {currency: 'USD', amount: 49.00}, props: {plan: 'Pro'}})
```

This lets you filter the revenue report by `plan` to compare revenue from different product lines.

**Where to fire the event**

Fire the revenue event on your order confirmation or thank you page, not on the checkout button click. Firing on button click captures intent but not completed purchases, which inflates revenue figures and makes attribution misleading.

For subscription upgrades, fire on the confirmation page after payment is processed, not when the user selects a plan.

**Count each purchase only once**

Thank-you pages get reloaded, bookmarked and reopened. Every time the purchase event fires again, it adds another conversion and more revenue. Use one of these:

Thank-you pages get reloaded, bookmarked and reopened. Every time the purchase event fires again, it adds another conversion and more revenue. Use one of these:

- **Remove the trigger from the URL after sending.** If your page sends the event only when the URL carries a checkout ID or amount, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` right after `plausible(...)`. A reload then has nothing to send. No storage needed.
- **Send from a callback, not a page.** Overlay checkouts (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy) fire their success callback once per payment.
- **Ignore old checkouts on the server.** When you look up the payment on your server, skip the event if the payment was created long ago (for example, Stripe's Checkout Session `created` timestamp is more than an hour old).
- **Mark the order in your own store.** If you already keep orders in a database, you can mark an order as tracked the first time the thank-you page renders, like our WordPress plugin does for WooCommerce orders. Nothing extra is sent to Plausible.

question: i added the class plausible-event-name=Button+Click on my button and made a goal called Button+Click but it shows zero conversions
reference_answer: The goal name must match the event name exactly, including capitalisation. The `+` in the class name is replaced with a space, so the class `plausible-event-name=Button+Click` sends the event `Button Click`. A goal named `Button+Click` won't count anything, so name it `Button Click`.
key_facts: Goal name must match the event name character for character
The + in the class name becomes a space
The event name here is `Button Click`
answer: The most common mismatch comes from the `+` sign in CSS class names, where the class `plausible-event-name=Button+Click` sends the event name `Button Click` with the plus replaced by a space [1]. If you created a goal called `Button+Click` instead of `Button Click`, nothing will be counted [1].
